lesson.title: SHOUTING_CASE: The Naming Convention Behind Constants
lesson.summary: A constant is a variable meant to hold a fixed value that should not change while a program runs, and Python signals that intent through an ALL_CAPS naming convention rather than any actual enforcement built into the language.
lesson.body:
Many programs rely on values that are meant to stay fixed for the entire run of the program, such as a tax rate, a maximum allowed score, or a physical constant like the acceleration due to gravity. Python calls a variable used this way a constant, but it is important to understand that Python has no separate const keyword the way some other languages do. A constant in Python is an ordinary variable; what makes it a constant is entirely the intent behind it and a naming convention that signals that intent to anyone reading the code.

That convention is to write the variable name in all uppercase letters, with underscores separating words: TAX_RATE = 0.08, MAX_ATTEMPTS = 3, GRAVITY = 9.8. These names still have to follow the same identifier rules covered in Variable Naming Rules, starting with a letter or underscore and containing no spaces; the convention simply adds the extra rule of writing every letter uppercase, on top of the rules that already apply to every variable name.

Trace a small example that uses a constant inside a calculation: GRAVITY = 9.8, followed by distance = 0.5 * GRAVITY * time ** 2. If time is 3, operator precedence evaluates the exponent first, 3 ** 2, giving 9. Then the multiplications run left to right: 0.5 * 9.8 gives 4.9, and 4.9 * 9 gives 44.1, so distance ends up 44.1. GRAVITY behaves exactly like any other variable in this expression; only its all-caps name marks it as a value the programmer intends to leave untouched for the rest of the program.

The value of this convention is entirely about communication between people, since the Python interpreter itself treats GRAVITY = 9.8 no differently than treating gravity = 9.8. When a teammate, a grader, or your future self sees MAX_ATTEMPTS written in all caps near the top of a file, the naming immediately signals do not reassign this partway through the program, and it also signals where to look if that value ever needs to change: one clearly named line at the top, rather than a scattered collection of unexplained numbers like 3 typed directly into several different places in the code.

It is worth being direct about the limitation: Python will not raise an error or stop the program if code later writes MAX_ATTEMPTS = 50, even accidentally. Unlike a compiler-enforced constant in some other languages, Python's constants are enforced only by convention, by the discipline of the programmer, and by anyone reviewing the code noticing the violation, not by the interpreter itself.

In practice, constants are usually gathered near the top of a file, before any of the code that uses them, so a reader can see every fixed value a program depends on in one place without hunting through the rest of the file. A program that calculates several students' final grades might define PASSING_GRADE = 60 once at the top and then compare against that name throughout, rather than typing the literal number 60 directly into several different comparisons; if the passing threshold ever changes, only that one line needs to be edited, and every calculation that depends on it updates automatically the next time the program runs.
